research_concepts: shot mix (rim, midrange, three-point shares from shot distance and shot type)
positive-control / design-sensitivity check for a lineup and matchup framework
substitution rotation intervals and stint construction
player-level shot profiles as the expected-composition benchmark
game state, opponent and fatigue confounding of within-game lineup changes
methodological_questions: Is 'changing the five moves shot mix' informative as a positive control, or is it nearly guaranteed because different players take different shots?
Can a pre-specified, player-profile-based expected shift in shot mix be compared with the observed shift, so the control tests calibration rather than mere non-zero change?
How can lineup-change events be isolated (for example, one-player swaps) from game state, opponent lineup, clock, fatigue and coach-timed substitutions?
Are stints long enough, and are lineup-change events plentiful enough, for stable shot-mix estimates?
Which placebo or negative-control comparisons (no-change windows, shuffled lineup labels) show the design does not produce shot-mix shifts without a personnel change?
Is shot mix independent of shot outcome, and how reliable is shot-distance coding?
evidence_establishes: No historical evidence was available: retrieve_history returned an empty list, so there are no prior records, statuses or failed approaches to cite.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether this project has previously tested lineup-change effects on shot mix.
Whether any earlier lineup/matchup design was validated, failed or shown to be an artifact.
Any effect sizes, variance estimates or pitfalls specific to this data.
own_inferences: As worded, the claim is close to tautological. Swapping players with different shot profiles (for example a rim-running big for a perimeter guard) will change the aggregate shot mix almost by construction. A non-zero shift therefore shows little about the design's ability to detect subtler personnel or matchup effects.

The control is informative only if the sign and approximate size of the shift are predicted in advance from player-level shot profiles estimated out of sample, and the observed shift tracks that prediction (dose-response).

A pure null is very unlikely if power is adequate. A failure would more likely point to an implementation or labeling problem, such as rotation intervals misaligned with play-by-play, than to a real absence of personnel effects.
One-player swaps within a game give a cleaner quasi-experimental contrast than comparing different five-man units across games. Five-man units rarely repeat often enough for stable estimates.
Substitutions are endogenous: fouls, injuries, fatigue, garbage time, timeouts and opponent adjustments all trigger them. A naive before/after comparison will mix personnel effects with these causes.
With around 3,700 or more games, aggregate power for swap-level contrasts is probably ample. Per-lineup, per-stint and per-matchup power will be poor.
uncertainties: The exact number of usable one-player-swap events is unknown until the rotation data are inspected.
The quality of alignment between substitution intervals and play-by-play clock is unknown.
The reliability of shot-distance and sub-type coding across seasons and in the playoffs is unknown.
It is unclear what the 'design' being validated is, for example a matchup-minutes model or a lineup-contrast model. The positive control's relevance depends on this.
Rule or style drift across the three seasons could change baseline shot mix.

prior_work.summary: No earlier project work was retrieved, so whether this positive control was already run is unknown.

risks.text: A shot-mix shift after a personnel change is largely guaranteed by the players' differing shot profiles. A bare 'shot mix changes' result would not show the design is sensitive. The control needs a predicted magnitude and direction, and a dose-response check.
Substitution timing correlates with score margin, foul trouble, fatigue, clock, opponent lineup and garbage time. These alter shot mix independently of who is on the floor.
Substitutions are triggered by performance or events such as cold streaks, fouls or injuries. Pre-change windows are therefore a selected, non-representative sample.
Five-man units rarely repeat, and stints contain few shot attempts. Per-lineup estimates are noisy, so the analysis must pool across swap events.
Shot-mix proportions on small attempt counts are highly variable. Shot-distance bins depend on tracking and coding quality.
Without no-change placebo windows, a detected 'effect' cannot be separated from within-game drift in shot mix (for example, pace or fatigue over the period).
Rotation intervals may not align precisely with play-by-play substitution events and clock. Possessions could then be assigned to the wrong five, especially around dead balls and period breaks.
League shot mix and rotation habits shift across seasons, and regular-season and playoff rotations differ. Pooled estimates could be biased unless season and stage are modeled.
Several shot-zone shares and many subgroups of swap types create a multiplicity risk unless the primary outcomes are fixed in advance.

design.estimand: For one-player swaps in the offensive five, the within-game change in the shot-zone distribution of team field-goal attempts (primary: rim share and three-point share). It is compared with the change predicted from the incoming and outgoing players' out-of-sample shot profiles, and with the same quantity in matched no-change placebo windows. The control passes if the observed shift (a) is nonzero in the predicted direction, (b) scales with the predicted shift (slope near 1, or at least positive and monotone across deciles of predicted shift), and (c) is absent in placebo windows.
design.unit: Lineup-change event (stint pair): the post-swap stint of the offensive five versus the pre-swap stint of the same team in the same game, with only one of the five players changed. Possessions or shot attempts are nested within events, and events within teams, games and seasons.
design.sample: All 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular-season and playoff games in the per-game files. Include one-player swaps where both adjacent stints have at least a pre-specified minimum of team FGA (for example 6, set before looking at outcomes). Exclude garbage time (a pre-specified margin and clock rule), overtime, end-of-period heaves and the first and last possession around the substitution if clock alignment is uncertain. Rotation intervals are reconciled with play-by-play substitution events, and mismatches are dropped and counted.
design.power: Compute the number of eligible swap events and the within-event variance of shot-zone shares before analysis, using a prior season or a held-out split for the variance. Pre-specify the minimum detectable shift in rim and three-point share at 80% power with cluster-robust SEs (clustered by game and team). Require the predicted-shift slope to be estimable with a CI half-width of at most 0.25. If the eligible events fall short, widen the minimum-FGA rule or pool the seasons. Do not lower the standard.
design.controls: Expected shot profiles are estimated from players' shots in held-out games (for example previous season or other-half-of-season), never from the test stint. Covariates: score margin, period, game clock, home/away, opponent, rest and back-to-back, foul counts, and the opponent's on-court composition where available. Include season and stage (regular season vs playoffs) fixed effects and game fixed effects, since each event is a within-game contrast. Run a sensitivity analysis excluding injury- or foul-driven swaps (for example, via ejections or an injury note where it can be inferred), and an analysis restricted to swaps made at stoppages.
design.falsification: (1) Placebo events: pseudo-changes at randomly chosen times within stints with no lineup change, matched on period and clock, should show a shift near 0 and no relation to the predicted shift. (2) Permutation test: shuffle incoming-player profiles across events within game and compare the slope against the null. (3) Negative-control outcome: a measure unrelated to who is playing, such as free-throw attempt share or the share of shots in the final 4 seconds of the shot clock if available, should not shift. (4) Check that the result holds when the players' profile is built only from prior-season data, so it does not rest on the same shots being tested.
design.multiplicity: Two primary outcomes, rim share and three-point share, with Holm correction. Midrange share is secondary and descriptive. Swap-type subgroups (guard-for-big, wing-for-wing, and so on) are exploratory and labeled as such, with no confirmatory inference.
design.decision_rule: Declare the positive control passed if both primary outcomes show a Holm-adjusted significant shift in the predicted direction, the predicted-shift slope has a CI that excludes 0 and includes values near 1 (or is monotone and positive), and the placebo shift and negative-control outcomes are indistinguishable from 0 within pre-specified equivalence bounds. If the main shift is present but the slope or placebo fails, classify the result as an artifact and do not treat the design as validated. If the minimum detectable effect exceeds the predicted effect, report the control as inconclusive rather than failed.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files (play-by-play, substitution rotation intervals, starters, box-score summary) for 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25 regular season and playoffs, as available on 2026-11-02. Derived play-type possession records from the graph database are used only as secondary descriptors. Record the file hashes or the database build date, the exclusion counts and the code commit before analysis.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm noting that the retrieval came back empty, so there's no historical evidence to draw on and I'll say so in the answer. The design question is a positive control: does changing the five offensive players move shot mix? I'm concerned it's nearly tautological, since different players have different shot profiles, so a positive control only means something if the outcome isn't close to guaranteed.

I'm checking whether a positive control holds up here, since a lineup change shifting shot mix might be nearly guaranteed because players have different shot profiles. I'd also need to account for confounders like game state, fatigue, and opponent lineup, and calibrate the expected shift to a specific effect size, such as a center-for-guard swap moving rim and three-point shares. Single-player swaps in stints would isolate the effect better, since full five-man lineups rarely repeat.

I'm planning placebo checks too: pseudo-changes at random times where the lineup stays the same, plus permuting lineup labels within each game. The sample is roughly three seasons of regular-season and playoff games, with many thousands of substitutions, though each stint only yields around ten to fifteen shots, so I'll need to aggregate heavily.

I'm settling on the risk codes for the design: mechanical floor, confounding, sparse exposure per stint, placebo dependence, regression to the mean from fouls or performance-driven substitutions, and label errors in shot distance or substitution timing. I'll keep the list to those that matter here and proceed with the planned changes.
